extracted.intended_audience: painters, poets, writers, and art connoisseurs interested in aesthetic and stylistic guidance
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and philosophical guidance on composing poetry and painting: how to interpret 'imitate nature', when to favour simplicity or ornament, how to choose style (grand vs literal), and how to portray character in writing. Focuses on aesthetic choices and common artistic anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Easy poetry / simplicity and naked elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce lines 'graced only by naked elegance and simple purity' rather than volumes 'swelled with epithets, brightened by figures, and stiffened by transpositions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson argues that true 'easy poetry' is scarce and harder to write than highly embellished verse: 'To require from any author many pieces of easy poetry, would be indeed to oppress him with too hard a task.' Anti-patterns: swollen lines full of epithets and forced transpositions are easier but inferior; scoring note: maintaining simple purity for many lines is especially difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid transpositions and harshness from remote thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of forced word-order changes ('transpositions') and harsh expressions when pursuing remote or affected thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes poets (e.g., Waller) who are 'too frequently driven into transpositions' and notes Cowley's remote thought led to 'harshness of expression.' Anti-pattern: syntactic contortions that impede clarity and naturalness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret 'imitate nature' as capturing universal ideas, not mere relief
rubrics_metrics.description: The maxim 'Imitate nature' should not be taken to mean literal, mechanical relief that merely makes objects seem real; rather, the painter of genius studies nature to exercise the imagination and capture invariable, general ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson: 'I know none who have explained in what manner this rule is to be understood...every one takes it in the most obvious sense...objects are represented naturally when they have such relief that they seem real.' He argues the painter of genius 'studies nature, and often arrives at his end, even by being unnatural in the confined sense of the word.' Anti-pattern: equating virtuoso technical copying with the highest excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand style: avoid minute naturalism in high art
rubrics_metrics.description: The grand style requires avoiding minute attention to petty particulars; greatness in painting (and poetry) arises from treating the great and general ideas rather than literal detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson contrasts the 'grand style' (focused on universal ideas) with detailed Dutch naturalness: 'Poetical ornaments destroy that air of truth and plainness which ought to characterize history; but the very being of poetry consists in departing from this plain narration.' Example: Michael Angelo's power would be diminished by adding mechanical, minute realism. Anti-pattern: overloading sublime work with small, distracting particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain stylistic consistency; do not combine incompatible excellencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not attempt to unite contrarieties of style (e.g., Dutch literal exactness with Italian grand manner); such mixtures destroy the efficacy of each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson warns: 'To desire to see the excellencies of each style united, to mingle the Dutch with the Italian school, is to join contrarieties which cannot subsist together.' Practical rule: pick the appropriate register (minute realism vs idealized generality) and remain coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the most general/typical form when selecting subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: When choosing a form to represent (in painting or description), select the most general or typical form—the invariable central form produced by nature—rather than accidental oddities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson: 'he selects, as the painter does, the most beautiful, that is, the most general form of nature.' He compares varieties to pendulums crossing a centre; the artist should pick the central, repeated form. Practical implication: idealize toward type, not isolate anomalies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the role of habit and custom in judgments of beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Many preferences of beauty arise from habit, custom, and repeated exposure rather than immutable formal criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson argues that liking is often a function of familiarity: 'custom makes, in a certain sense, white black, and black white' and that racial/cultural standards of beauty are shaped by custom. Implication for artists: be aware that audience taste is conditioned and not purely objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty evokes admiration but is not equivalent to beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty can make something admired because it is uncommon, but uncommonness alone does not constitute beauty in form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson distinguishes admiration from formal beauty: 'Novelty is said to be one of the causes of beauty: that novelty is a very sufficient reason why we should admire, is not denied; but, because it is uncommon, is it, therefore, beautiful?' Use novelty carefully—it may attract attention but not solve formal aesthetic problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate enthusiasm: balance imagination and restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should admit some enthusiasm—an intimate knowledge of the passions and good sense must determine how much imagination to allow; too much produces incoherence, too little produces lifeless insipidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson: 'There may...be too great an indulgence, as well as too great a restraint of imagination...An intimate knowledge of the passions, and good sense, but not common sense, must at last determine its limits.' Example/anti-pattern: Michael Angelo sometimes transgressed limits into the ridiculous; modern painters need more enthusiasm but within bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing mechanical skill with liberal-art greatness
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical facility in imitating surface truth is distinct from the liberal, imaginative excellence that makes painting a sister to poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson: 'this imitation being merely mechanical, in which the slowest intellect is always sure to succeed best...the painter of genius cannot stoop to drudgery, in which the understanding has no part.' Practical test: does a work engage imagination and convey universal ideas, or merely show faithful surface detail?

rubrics_metrics.name: Character sketching: portray striking habitual traits through speech and behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: When sketching characters, present distinctive, repeatable conversational habits and mannerisms (e.g., Tom Steady's uncontroverted assertions, Will Startle's exclamations, Jack Solid's quotations) so the type is immediately recognizable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay offers many exemplars — show, don't tell: let a character's repeated speech patterns and habits (vehement assertion, sententiousness, quotation, hyper-sensibility, pedantic explanation) reveal their type. Use economy: a few well-chosen traits make a convincing sketch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reductive or one-note characterisation when undesired
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of making characters mere rhetorical devices (only repeating aphorisms, only quoting, or only contradicting) unless the one-note is the point of satire or comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern examples: Bob Sturdy (stubborn repetition without reasons), Jack Solid (totally given to quotations), Dick Wormwood (always finding fault). If used, these should be purposeful and clearly comic or critical rather than lazy portraiture.

rubrics_metrics.name: In argument or dialogue, provide reasons not mere repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely repeating an assertion (as Bob Sturdy does) is a rhetorical vice; sound discourse should supply reasons and respond to objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson criticises the tactic of wearing down opponents by reiteration: 'without troubling himself to search for reasons, he tires his antagonist with repeated affirmations.' For persuasive writing/dialogue, require substantiation rather than brute assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use temperament and diction suited to the subject's register
rubrics_metrics.description: Match vocabulary, gestures, and emotional display to the character or subject: excessive exclamations and extreme vocabulary (Will Startle) are appropriate to hyper-sensitive types but would be misplaced elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Johnson lists how types differ (sensibility, sententiousness, research-driven explanation); when writing, choose diction and expressive devices that fit the psychological profile and avoid misapplied mannerisms that break verisimilitude.
